description: Buddhist attitudes to death, mourning, rebirth, the six realms, Bardo, Obon and impermanence.
content_html:
Buddhism and Death: Impermanence at Its Sharpest

Death is not a taboo in Buddhism; it is one of the central facts that the tradition asks practitioners to face directly. The Buddha taught that impermanence (anicca) applies to everything, including the self. Death is simply the most visible expression of this universal truth. The Dhammapada teaches: “Just as a flower, fair and lovely, but without fragrance, the well-spoken word bears no fruit for one who does not act upon it” (Dhammapada 51–52) — and more directly in the tradition associated with Dhammapada 37: “The river flows on; the moon waxes and wanes; so too does life” (the broader Dhammapada tradition on impermanence). The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Buddha’s first teaching, establishes that dukkha — unsatisfactoriness — is bound up with change, ageing and death: these are not failures of existence but its fundamental nature.

Kamma, Rebirth and the Six Realms of Existence

Kamma (Sanskrit: karma) is the engine of rebirth. Every intentional action — bodily, verbal or mental — generates a volitional force that shapes the nature of future experience. At death, this accumulated kamma influences the conditions of the next rebirth. In both Theravada and Mahayana traditions, the universe is understood to contain six realms of existence into which beings are reborn based on their kamma:

The six realms are: (1) the realm of gods (devas), a pleasant but impermanent state; (2) the realm of demi-gods (asuras), characterised by jealousy and conflict; (3) the human realm — considered the most favourable for achieving liberation; (4) the animal realm; (5) the realm of hungry ghosts (pretas), beings tormented by insatiable craving; and (6) the hell realms, states of intense suffering. The Tibetan Wheel of Life (Bhavachakra) depicts all six realms enclosed within the grasp of Yama, the lord of death, symbolising that all realms without exception are subject to impermanence.

Key Fact

Buddhism teaches six realms of existence into which beings are reborn based on kamma: gods, demi-gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts and hell realms. The human realm is considered the most favourable for achieving nibbana because humans can practise the Dhamma, experience both pleasure and suffering, and make intentional choices.

Death and Mourning in Theravada Communities

In Theravada communities (such as those in Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar), death rituals focus on generating and transferring merit to the deceased. When a person dies, monks are invited to the home to chant protective texts (paritta). The body is washed and prepared. Cremation is the norm, reflecting the Buddhist teaching on impermanence and the lack of a permanent self. The funeral sermon emphasises the Dhamma and the reality of impermanence, encouraging mourners not to cling to the deceased. During the period of mourning, merit-making activities such as offering food to monks or donating to a temple are performed on behalf of the dead, with the belief that the merit generated can improve their conditions in the next life. Dhammapada 170–171 teaches that one who sees the world as a bubble and a mirage is not seen by the king of death — pointing to the liberating effect of seeing through the illusion of permanence.

Tibetan Buddhism has a highly developed understanding of the dying process, recorded in the Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol). The text was compiled by the treasure-revealer Karma Lingpa in the 14th century and describes the experience of the consciousness after death during the Bardo — the transitional period between death and rebirth.

In Tibetan belief, at the moment of death the consciousness experiences a clear white light (clear light of dharmata). If the person recognises this light as their own true nature — the Buddha-nature within — they are liberated from rebirth. If they do not recognise it (due to the obscurations created by kamma), they progress through further Bardo stages, encountering peaceful and wrathful deities. These deities are understood as projections of the person’s own mind. A lama (monk-teacher) reads the Bardo Thodol aloud to the dying and recently deceased to guide consciousness towards liberation. After 49 days, consciousness takes rebirth in one of the six realms.

The Tibetan practice represents a distinctly Mahayana and Vajrayana understanding of death, contrasting with Theravada practice where chanting and merit-making are the principal responses to death.

Key Fact

The Bardo is the intermediate state between death and rebirth in Tibetan Buddhist teaching, lasting up to 49 days. The Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol) is read aloud by a lama to guide the consciousness through the Bardo, helping it recognise the clear light of Buddha-nature and achieve liberation rather than taking an unfavourable rebirth.

Obon: Japanese Buddhist Death Festival

In Japan, the Buddhist festival of Obon is observed in mid-August (or July in some regions). Obon derives from the Sanskrit Ullambana Sutra, which tells of the monk Maudgalyayana using the power of the Sangha to release his deceased mother from the hungry-ghost realm. During Obon, it is believed that the spirits of deceased ancestors return to visit the family home. Families clean ancestral graves, light lanterns to guide the spirits back, and place offerings of food and flowers before the home altar. The festival culminates in traditional bon odori (Obon dances) and the floating of lit paper lanterns on rivers or out to sea, symbolically guiding the spirits back to the spirit world. Obon illustrates how local Japanese culture has shaped Buddhist practice: the festival blends Buddhist concepts of merit and the realm of hungry ghosts with pre-existing Japanese ancestor veneration.

All three traditions share the same foundational beliefs: death is governed by kamma; rebirth follows; the goal is to escape the cycle through enlightenment. However, the ritual responses differ significantly due to both doctrinal and cultural variation. Theravada communities use merit-transfer, monk-chanting and cremation. Tibetan communities use the Bardo Thodol, prostrations, and a 49-day ritual period. Japanese Obon integrates ancestor veneration with Buddhist beliefs about the hungry-ghost realm.

The Dhammapada verse 37 points to the universal Buddhist concern: just as the mind travels through life, so it travels after death. The practical implication is that a well-practised mind — one trained in the Eightfold Path — is better prepared for the experience of dying and what follows. This is why meditation in life is understood to have direct consequences for the experience of death, wherever in the Buddhist world this belief is held.
exam_tip_html: When answering an “Explain” (6 marks) question on Buddhist attitudes to death, make sure you name the tradition (Theravada, Tibetan or Mahayana/Japanese) and explain both the ritual and the belief it expresses. A common error is treating Obon as a non-Buddhist folk festival — always connect it to the Buddhist teaching on the realm of hungry ghosts and merit. For the 15-mark Discuss, you can use the contrast between Theravada and Tibetan approaches as two developed perspectives. Accurate spelling of Bardo, kamma, impermanence and Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is rewarded in extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Buddhism teaches that death is the most visible expression of impermanence (anicca). Kamma drives rebirth into one of six realms; the human realm is considered most favourable for achieving liberation. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta establishes that ageing and death are inherent in conditioned existence.
  • Theravada communities respond to death with monk-chanting, merit-transfer and cremation; Tibetan Buddhism uses the Bardo Thodol (Tibetan Book of the Dead) to guide consciousness through the 49-day intermediate state (Bardo). Japanese Buddhism observes Obon, honouring the returning spirits of ancestors.
  • All Buddhist traditions share the belief that meditation practice in life prepares the mind for death, and that kamma accumulated through ethical action shapes what follows death. Local culture shapes the ritual expression of these shared beliefs.

practice_questions.text: State one belief Buddhists hold about what happens after death.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: consciousness is reborn in one of the six realms / kamma determines the nature of rebirth / the Bardo is an intermediate state between death and rebirth / death is governed by the principle of impermanence (anicca). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Bardo is in Tibetan Buddhist teaching.
practice_questions.marks: The Bardo is the intermediate state between death and rebirth [1]; it is a period (up to 49 days) during which the consciousness experiences visions, including a clear white light representing Buddha-nature, and has the opportunity to achieve liberation or take a new rebirth [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of the Tibetan Book of the Dead for Tibetan Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol) is a text read aloud by a lama to the dying and recently deceased [1]; it guides consciousness through the Bardo by describing the visions it will encounter and how to recognise them as projections of the mind [1]; its purpose is to help the consciousness achieve liberation by recognising the clear light of Buddha-nature rather than being drawn into an unfavourable rebirth [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Buddhist beliefs about kamma and rebirth influence attitudes to death and mourning.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Kamma means that actions performed in life shape the conditions of the next rebirth — this leads Theravada communities to perform merit-transfer rituals (offering food to monks, donating to temples) on behalf of the deceased, with the belief that generated merit can benefit the dead. This reflects the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta's teaching that intentional action has consequences.
• Belief in the six realms of existence means that mourners may act to help the deceased achieve a favourable rebirth. In Tibetan Buddhism, the Bardo Thodol is read to help consciousness avoid the lower realms and ideally achieve liberation.
• Belief in impermanence (anicca) shapes the tone of mourning — clinging to the dead is seen as harmful since it is rooted in the delusion that things persist. The Dhammapada 170–171 teaches that one who sees the world as a bubble is not trapped by death's power.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 simple point, 2 developed, 3 with teaching/source]

practice_questions.text: 'Buddhist death rituals are more about the living than the dead.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Merit-transfer rituals, chanting and offerings comfort the bereaved and reinforce community bonds, giving mourners a sense of purposeful action. The gathering of monks and community at a Theravada funeral serves to strengthen the lay sangha.
• The Obon festival in Japan is clearly a communal and social event, with family gatherings, dances and lanterns — it can be argued that remembering and honouring ancestors serves the psychological needs of the living as much as the dead.
• The emphasis in Buddhist teachings on impermanence is directed at the living: Dhammapada 170–171 uses death as a teaching tool to encourage the living to practise the Dhamma now.

Arguments against:
• Tibetan Buddhist practice is explicitly oriented towards helping the consciousness of the deceased navigate the Bardo. The Bardo Thodol is read to the dead, not the living, and its aim is to improve the deceased's rebirth or achieve their liberation.
• Theravada merit-transfer believes generated merit can genuinely influence the next life of the deceased — this is a sincere belief that the rituals benefit the dead, not merely the living.
• The six realms doctrine holds that beings in lower realms (hungry ghosts, hell realms) genuinely need help; practices aimed at transferring merit or guiding consciousness are understood as having real effects on the deceased.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with Theravada/Tibetan/Japanese comparison, named teachings (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Bardo Thodol, Dhammapada), explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with some Buddhist content and teaching; conclusion offered.
Developing: One side stronger; some relevant Buddhist content; limited source references.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no Buddhist teaching. [15 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Obon for Japanese Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Obon is a Japanese festival observed in mid-August in which it is believed the spirits of deceased ancestors return to visit the family home [1]; families clean graves, light lanterns to guide spirits back, place offerings before the home altar and perform traditional Obon dances [1]; the festival connects Buddhist beliefs about the realm of hungry ghosts and merit with Japanese ancestor veneration, showing the influence of local culture on Buddhist practice [1]. [3 marks]

What is the Bardo in Tibetan Buddhist teaching?
options: A Tibetan word for the six realms of existence
The intermediate state between death and rebirth lasting up to 49 days
A form of Tibetan meditation on impermanence
The Tibetan equivalent of the Theravada Pali Canon

knowledge_checks.q: The Japanese Buddhist festival of _____ honours the spirits of deceased ancestors, who are believed to return briefly to the family home.

right: Monk-chanting, merit-transfer and cremation to benefit the deceased
Reading the Bardo Thodol to guide consciousness through the 49-day intermediate state

flashcard_questions.a: The principle that intentional actions shape future experience in this and future lives.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six realms of existence in Buddhism.
flashcard_questions.a: Gods, demi-gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell realms.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the human realm considered most favourable in Buddhism?
flashcard_questions.a: Humans can practise the Dhamma, experience both pleasure and suffering, and make intentional choices.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Tibetan Book of the Dead?
flashcard_questions.a: A text (Bardo Thodol) read to the dying to guide consciousness through the intermediate state (Bardo).
The intermediate state between death and rebirth in Tibetan teaching, lasting up to 49 days.

flashcard_questions.q: What opportunity does the Bardo provide?
flashcard_questions.a: To recognise the clear light of Buddha-nature and achieve liberation from rebirth.
A Japanese Buddhist festival honouring ancestor spirits believed to return to the family home.

flashcard_questions.q: How do Theravada communities help the deceased at death?
flashcard_questions.a: By inviting monks to chant protective texts, performing merit-transfer and cremating the body.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sutta established that death and ageing are part of the nature of conditioned existence?
flashcard_questions.a: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (the Buddha's first teaching at Sarnath).

flashcard_questions.q: What do Dhammapada 170–171 teach about death?
flashcard_questions.a: One who sees the world as a bubble and mirage is not seen by the king of death — impermanence is liberating.

flashcard_questions.q: How does local culture affect Buddhist death rituals?
flashcard_questions.a: It shapes the specific practices — e.g. Obon blends Buddhist and Japanese ancestor veneration.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Theravada communities perform merit-transfer after a death?
flashcard_questions.a: Because kamma shapes rebirth — merit generated on behalf of the dead may benefit their next life.

glossary_terms.definition: The Buddhist teaching (anicca) that all conditioned phenomena are constantly changing; one of the Three Marks of Existence.
The Pali term for the Buddhist principle that intentional actions generate consequences shaping future experience in this and future lives.
The cycle of birth, death and re-arising driven by kamma and craving, from which Buddhism seeks liberation.
A Tibetan Buddhist text (Bardo Thodol) read aloud to the dying and recently dead to guide consciousness through the intermediate state.
The intermediate state between death and rebirth in Tibetan Buddhist teaching, during which consciousness has opportunities to achieve liberation.
A Japanese Buddhist festival held in mid-August to honour the spirits of deceased ancestors, who are believed to return briefly to the family home.
The Elder school of Buddhism, predominant in South and South-East Asia, emphasising individual liberation and the Pali Canon.
